message.content:
## The Bottle at Blackrock

Blackrock Lighthouse stood three hundred feet above the Atlantic, on a column of basalt that the sea claimed whenever the tide rose high enough. Thomas Ellery had kept the light there since 1955. He was fifty-seven years old, born in 1901, and he remembered his father, William, speaking of the place before William died in 1930. William had been Blackrock’s keeper from 1904 until his retirement, though he never spoke often of the winter of that year.

On September 14, 1958, Thomas went down to the shore after the evening watch. The wind had driven the sea against the rocks all night, and when he reached the tide line, something green lay half buried in the seaweed.

It was a bottle, its neck sealed with wax. The glass was old and slightly warped, but the label inside was legible. It read: **HMS Vulture, 1904**.

Thomas knew the name. William had once told him that the Vulture had fallen out of the weather that November, with no survivor whose body was ever found. The ship had been lost without a trace, and the logbook at Blackrock had recorded only that the light had been kept through the gale.

Thomas carried the bottle up the stairs. He broke the seal at the lantern room, where the great lens turned above him, and unfolded the paper. It was written in ink that had faded to brown.

> **November 3, 1904**
>
> Captain Henry Bell wrote these words. The Vulture is gone. I do not know whether anyone will find this. The compass has turned toward the rocks, and I cannot trust it further. If you read this, do not follow the compass. Follow the light, even if the light is far from where you expect it.
>
> **Henry Bell**

Thomas turned the paper over. On the back was a single position: **57°14′N, 6°28′W**.

He had read the same position in the ship’s log that his father had left behind. The coordinates lay beneath the water, far from Blackrock, where the Vulture had been last reported. But the letter said something else. **Follow the light, even if the light is far from where you expect it.**

William had kept the light through that gale. Thomas had always assumed his father had remained at the station because that was his duty. Now he wondered whether William had known more than he had told.

Thomas wrote a reply on the back of the paper.

> **September 14, 1958**
>
> Blackrock is lit. The light is here.
>
> **Thomas Ellery**

He put the bottle back on the desk beside the logbook. He did not send it. There was no ship to send it to, and no one at that position who could answer. The sea had kept its secret for fifty-four years. To throw it back would be to begin the same journey again.

The next morning, September 15, 1958, Thomas climbed to the lantern room with a cup of coffee. The glass had been cleaned the night before, and the lens threw a white beam across the water every twelve seconds. For a moment he saw something move below.

A small boat was drifting toward the rocks.

Thomas ran through the gallery and turned the alarm bell. He did not know how many were aboard. He could only see one figure at the tiller, leaning over as if trying to make the boat respond. The compass on the boat was turning slowly, then stopped, then turned again toward the rocks.

Thomas understood the message before he understood anything else.

He called the Coastguard at once. His voice was steady, although his hands were not. He gave the position, the number of the boat, and the direction in which it was moving. The Coastguard said they would send a vessel. They did not know how long it would take.

Thomas watched the boat. The figure looked up at the lighthouse once. The light was far from where he expected it, perhaps, because the man was looking for a harbour that did not exist on his chart. But the light was real.

The figure pulled something from the water. Thomas could not see what it was. It might have been a compass. It might have been another bottle.

The Coastguard boat arrived at 09:40. The figure was brought aboard. The man said his name was not Henry Bell. He said he had found the bottle in the water before he found the lighthouse. He said he had followed the light because his compass would not work.

Thomas asked him about the paper. The man said he had read the message before he left the shore. He had not known who Henry Bell was. He had not known that the bottle was fifty-four years old.

Thomas did not ask whether the man had brought the bottle back. He did not ask whether the reply had been read.

Later, while the man was being taken to the hospital, Thomas returned to the lantern room. The bottle was still on the desk. The reply remained written on the back.

He opened the logbook and wrote a new entry.

> **September 15, 1958**
>
> The Vulture’s survivor was found. The light was followed. The compass did not work. I do not know whether Henry Bell ever reached the shore. I do not know whether the message was meant for him, or for someone who would read it long after he had died.
>
> The light is here.

Thomas closed the book. He looked out through the glass. The sea was calm now, although the wind had not yet stopped. Somewhere beneath it, the Vulture lay in the dark. The bottle lay on the desk.

Thomas did not throw it back. He did not know whether he would ever open it again. He knew only that the light must be kept, and that the message must not be treated as a ship’s log.

He lit the lamp again. The beam moved across the water, and for a moment the glass beneath it seemed to shine. Then the lens turned, and the light went out.

message.content:
I would not recommend a **per-keystroke productivity index** as a measure of developer performance. A single keystroke can change a type signature and ripple through many files; conversely, a large, high-value refactoring can have a low score because of the many keystrokes required. Thus such a metric rewards small changes, penalizes large work, and can easily be gamed.

A more defensible approach is to measure **value per change or per feature**, not per keystroke:

\[
\text{Contribution}_c = w_v v_c + w_q q_c - w_r r_c
\]

- \(v_c\): normalized value of the change (feature complete, tests added, documentation, code review approval)
- \(q_c\): quality measure (bugs introduced, review feedback, static-analysis issues)
- \(r_c\): rework or rollback
- \(w_v, w_q, w_r\): weights calibrated from outcomes, not arbitrarily chosen

Then:

\[
\text{Productivity}_d = \frac{\sum_{c \in \text{developer } d} \text{Contribution}_c}{\text{engineering\_time}_d}
\]

If you only want to measure **semantic density** as an exploratory tool—not for performance evaluation—you can approximate semantic impact from:

- files and modules affected
- call sites and type signatures changed
- tests added or modified
- breaking changes and post-merge incidents

\[
\text{SemanticDensity}_c = \frac{\sum_m w_m \cdot \text{reach}_m(c)}{k_{e,c} + \lambda k_{n,c}}
\]

where \(k_{e,c}\) is editing keystrokes, \(k_{n,c}\) is navigation/undo keystrokes, and \(\text{reach}_m(c)\) is the measured impact on module \(m\). Use this to compare editors, templates, or tooling, not to rank individuals.

Before using any version of this, validate it against actual outcomes, report it in aggregate, and do not tie it to pay or promotions without explicit consent and a validated calibration.

message.content:
This is the key update: **the 2015 patent, if BigCorp let it lapse in 2023 for nonpayment of a maintenance fee and it is listed as expired in the patent office database, no longer provides a basis for infringement claims in that jurisdiction.**

Do not conclude, however, that all legal risk has vanished. The risk from this patent is effectively removed; other active patents, other jurisdictions, reissue, design patents, trademarks or trade dress remain. So the **EV model** changes in **p** and **L**, not in its logic.

### 1. Updated decision rule

Push now, without redesign, if both conditions are met:

\[
\text{EV}_{\text{push}} > \text{EV}_{\text{pause}} \quad \text{and} \quad L_{\text{other}} \le \text{Cash available for worst-case event}
\]

If only the 2015 patent was the risk:

\[
p \approx 0, \quad L_{\text{2015}} \approx 0
\]

Then:

\[
\text{EV}_{\text{push}} \approx R
\]
\[
\text{EV}_{\text{pause}} = R(1-d) - C_{\text{FTO}}
\]

So the pause costs you **delay** and **FTO fee**, with no commensurate reduction in legal risk.

### 2. Working example

Using the same numbers, but assuming other active patents pose a risk of **0.5%** and total downside **$150,000**, instead of the old **1.5% / $300,000**:

| Path | EV | Downside |
|---|---:|---:|
| Push now | $139,250 | $150,000 |
| FTO only + pause | $122,650 | $150,000 |
| FTO + redesign | $82,200 | ~$90,000 |

Here, pushing now is worth **$16,600** more than an FTO-only pause and **$57,050** more than redesign. Redesign does not make sense for the 2015 patent; its $35,000** is spent to remove a risk that no longer exists.

### 3. What must be confirmed this week

Do not treat the database status as a final answer; confirm the following:

1. **Jurisdiction:** expiration in the US, not necessarily in the EU, UK, Canada or other jurisdictions where you sell.
2. **Status:** no reinstatement, no grace period, no pending reissue or continuation that could revive similar rights.
3. **Claims:** no other active patent, not just the 2015 patent.
4. **Contracts:** retailer IP indemnity, delivery penalties, cancellation rights and warranty language.
5. **FTO scope:** claim construction, invalidity search, non-infringement and willfulness, as well as the status of the 2015 patent.

The cost of this is roughly **$2,000–$5,000**; compared with the **$35,000** redesign, it is a small premium for certainty.

### 4. Recommended path

- **Confirmed expiration + no other active patents:** push now, do not pause production, do not redesign. Add FTO in parallel, not as a production gate.
- **Other active patent remains:** return to the prior model, but calculate **p** and **L** only for that patent.
- **Status uncertain:** pause only for the narrow FTO scope, not for redesign.

The advisor’s old argument is now incorrect in one part: **2–3+ years litigation timeline** does not apply to an expired patent. But it is still correct in the other: if **$150,000** (or another **L**) exceeds your cash runway, the solvency floor is violated and you must cap liability before pushing.

**Rule:** do not use the expiration to skip the FTO; use it to skip the redesign. If the FTO finds no other active risk, **FTO in parallel + production** is the best path.

def parse_nested_parens(paren_string: str) -> List[int]:
    """ Input to this function is a string represented multiple groups for nested parentheses separated by spaces.
    For each of the group, output the deepest level of nesting of parentheses.
    E.g. (()()) has maximum two levels of nesting while ((())) has three.

    >>> parse_nested_parens('(()()) ((())) () ((())()())')
    [2, 3, 1, 3]
    """
    groups = paren_string.split()
    result = []

        current_depth = 0
        max_depth = 0
        for char in group:

                max_depth = max(max_depth, current_depth)

def encode_cyclic(s: str):
    """
    returns encoded string by cycling groups of three characters.
    """
    # split string to groups. Each of length 3.
    groups = [s[(3 * i):min((3 * i + 3), len(s))] for i in range((len(s) + 2) // 3)]

    groups = [(group[1:] + group[0]) if len(group) == 3 else group for group in groups]

def is_palindrome(string: str) -> bool:
    """ Test if given string is a palindrome """
    return string == string[::-1]


def make_palindrome(string: str) -> str:
    """ Find the shortest palindrome that begins with a supplied string.
    Algorithm idea is simple:
    - Find the longest postfix of supplied string that is a palindrome.
    - Append to the end of the string reverse of a string prefix that comes before the palindromic suffix.
    >>> make_palindrome('')
    ''
    >>> make_palindrome('cat')
    'catac'
    >>> make_palindrome('cata')
    'catac'
    """
    if not string:
        return ""

    for i in range(len(string)):
        suffix = string[i:]
        if is_palindrome(suffix):
            prefix = string[:i]
            return string + prefix[::-1]

    return string

def encode_cyclic(s: str):
    """
    returns encoded string by cycling groups of three characters.
    """
    # split string to groups. Each of length 3.
    groups = [s[(3 * i):min((3 * i + 3), len(s))] for i in range((len(s) + 2) // 3)]

from typing import List


def parse_nested_parens(paren_string: str) -> List[int]:
    """ Input to this function is a string represented multiple groups for nested parentheses separated by spaces.
    For each of the group, output the deepest level of nesting of parentheses.
    E.g. (()()) has maximum two levels of nesting while ((())) has three.

    >>> parse_nested_parens('(()()) ((())) () ((())()())')
    [2, 3, 1, 3]
    """
    groups = paren_string.split()
    result = []

    for group in groups:
        current_depth = 0
        max_depth = 0

        for char in group:
            if char == '(':
                current_depth += 1
                if current_depth > max_depth:
                    max_depth = current_depth
            elif char == ')':
                current_depth -= 1

        result.append(max_depth)

    return result
```

from pathlib import Path
import shutil

def task_func(kwargs, target_dir="non_none_files"):
    """
    Process files from a dictionary by checking if the file exists,
    and if it has content, then copies it to a target directory.

    Args:
        kwargs: A dictionary mapping file names/keys to file paths.
        target_dir: The directory where files will be copied.

    Returns:
        copied_files: A list of full file paths that were copied.
    """
    copied_files = []
    target_path = Path(target_dir)
    target_path.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    for key, file_path in kwargs.items():
        file_path = Path(file_path)

        if not file_path.exists():
            continue

        if file_path.is_dir():
            continue

        file_size = file_path.stat().st_size
        if file_size == 0:
            continue

        dest_path = target_path / file_path.name
        shutil.copy2(file_path, dest_path)
        copied_files.append(str(dest_path.resolve()))

    return copied_files
```

import re
from datetime import datetime, time

def task_func(logs: list):
    timestamp_pattern = re.compile(
        r'(\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}\s+\d{2}:\d{2}:\d{2})',
        re.IGNORECASE
    )
    error_pattern = re.compile(r'error', re.IGNORECASE)
    error_times = []

    for log in logs:
        if not isinstance(log, str):
            continue
        if not error_pattern.search(log):
            continue
        match = timestamp_pattern.search(log)
        if not match:
            continue
        try:
            dt = datetime.strptime(match.group(1), '%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')
            error_times.append(dt)
        except ValueError:
            continue

    if not error_times:
        return [], None

    total_seconds = sum(
        t.hour * 3600 + t.minute * 60 + t.second
        for t in error_times
    )
    average_seconds = total_seconds / len(error_times)
    avg_hour = int(average_seconds // 3600)
    average_seconds %= 3600
    avg_minute = int(average_seconds // 60)
    avg_second = round(average_seconds % 60)

    return [
        t.strftime('%H:%M:%S')
        for t in error_times
    ], time(avg_hour, avg_minute, avg_second)
```

import csv

from random import randint

def task_func(hours, output_dir=OUTPUT_DIR):
    """
    Generate sensor data for the specified number of hours and save it in a CSV file.

    Args:

        output_dir (str): Directory where the CSV file will be saved.

    Returns:
        str: Path to the generated CSV file.
    """
    os.makedirs(output_dir, exist_ok=True)
    filepath = os.path.join(output_dir, 'sensor_data.csv')

        time = start_time + timedelta(hours=i)
        temperature = randint(15, 35)
        humidity = randint(30, 90)
        pressure = randint(980, 1020)

        data.append({
            'Time': time.isoformat(),
            'Temperature': temperature,
            'Humidity': humidity,
            'Pressure': pressure
        })

    with open(filepath, mode='w', newline='') as file:
        writer = csv.DictWriter(file, fieldnames=['Time', 'Temperature', 'Humidity', 'Pressure'])
        writer.writeheader()
        writer.writerows(data)

    return filepath
```

import os
import re
from pathlib import Path


def task_func(dir_path: str, predicates: list) -> dict:
    """
    Evaluates each file/directory name in dir_path against the provided predicates.

    Args:
        dir_path: Path to the directory to evaluate.
        predicates: List of predicates. Each predicate can be a callable that accepts
                    a filename and returns a boolean, or a non-empty string interpreted
                    as a regular expression pattern.

    Returns:
        A dictionary mapping each directory item name to a list of boolean results,
        one per deduplicated valid predicate, in order.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If no valid predicates are provided.
        FileNotFoundError: If dir_path does not exist or is not a directory.
    """
    path = Path(dir_path)

    if not path.exists() or not path.is_dir():
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"Directory not found or is not a directory: {dir_path}")

    def _normalize_predicate(pred):
        if callable(pred):
            return pred
        if isinstance(pred, str) and pred.strip():
            return re.compile(pred)
        return None

    # Filter to valid predicates
    valid_predicates = [p for p in predicates if _normalize_predicate(p) is not None]

    if not valid_predicates:
        raise ValueError("No valid predicates provided.")

    # Deduplicate: callables by identity, regex patterns by their pattern string
    seen = set()
    deduped = []

    for p in valid_predicates:
        if callable(p) and not isinstance(p, type(re.compile(""))):
            key = id(p)
        else:
            key = p.pattern

        if key not in seen:
            seen.add(key)
            deduped.append(p)

    result = {}

    for name in os.listdir(path):
        checks = []

        for pred in deduped:
            if callable(pred) and not isinstance(pred, type(re.compile(""))):
                checks.append(bool(pred(name)))
            else:
                checks.append(bool(pred.search(name)))

        result[name] = checks

    return result

message.content: Zoos should be abolished because they prioritize human entertainment over animal welfare. Captivity restricts animals' freedom, prevents natural behaviors, and inflicts psychological distress on creatures evolved to roam vast territories. No facility can recreate wild ecosystems or meet every species' social and physical needs. Rather than preserving endangered animals, many zoos rely on breeding programs keeping populations in enclosures, while genuine conservation requires protecting habitats and addressing poaching, climate change, and threats at their source. Funds spent on exhibits would be better invested in sanctuary networks and habitat preservation, allowing animals to live without observation. Abolishing zoos is not a rejection of appreciation; it acknowledges animals are not property to be displayed.
